references.text: The Mosaic law's command to help a brother's donkey or ox that has fallen: "If you see your brother's donkey or ox fall on the road, do not turn away from them. You must help him lift it up again" (Deut 22:4). Jesus uses a similar principle – saving an animal in distress – to justify healing on the Sabbath.

The command to help even an enemy's donkey that is lying under its burden: "When you see the donkey of someone who hates you lying under its load, do not leave it there, but help him unload it" (Exod 23:5). This shows that mercy toward animals in distress applied regardless of circumstances, an argument Jesus employs in his Sabbath teaching.

A parallel episode where Jesus argues for healing on the Sabbath by referring to daily care for animals: "You hypocrites! Does not each one of you untie his ox or donkey from the manger on the Sabbath and lead it out to give it water?" (Luke 13:15-16). The same type of argument from the lesser to the greater (kal va-chomer).

Jesus' corresponding argument in the Gospel of Matthew: "Which one of you, if he has a sheep that falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a person than a sheep!" (Matt 12:11-12). A direct parallel with the same "from the lesser to the greater" argument concerning healing on the Sabbath.

The immediate context where Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath and asks the Pharisees, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?" (Luke 14:1-4). Verse 5 is Jesus' follow-up argument after this healing.

Jesus uses a similar argument in John: If circumcision is performed on the Sabbath so that the Mosaic law is not broken, should not a whole person be made well on the Sabbath as well? (John 7:22-23). The same logical pattern that necessary actions are permitted on the Sabbath.

Jesus' question to the Pharisees in another Sabbath controversy: "Is it lawful to do good or to do evil on the Sabbath, to save life or to destroy it?" (Luke 6:9). Jesus establishes the principle that doing good is always right, even on the Sabbath.
